title: Synchronization for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers
problem: Logical qubits encoded with the surface code in fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQC) can become desynchronized across their syndrome generation cycles due to heterogeneous QEC codes (color, qLDPC), fabrication defects causing extended clock cycles, and modular chip-to-chip coupling latencies. Lattice Surgery merge operations require all involved patches to begin their next syndrome generation cycle in lockstep, so desynchronized patches must idle—accumulating decoherence errors—before the operation can proceed.
method: Three synchronization policies are defined for the surface code with Lattice Surgery: (1) Passive—leading patch idles for the full synchronization slack immediately before the merge; (2) Active—slack is distributed as small idle fragments inserted after every QEC round, so no single idle window accumulates large decoherence; (3) Hybrid—for patches with unequal cycle times, runs extra rounds of error correction to reduce the residual slack, then applies Active for the remainder. A hardware microarchitecture consisting of a Patch Counter Table, Phase Calculators, and a Synchronization Slack Calculator determines patch phases at runtime and injects barrier instructions into the QEC controller schedule without adding latency to the critical path.

title: DX100: Programmable Data Access Accelerator for Indirection
problem: Indirect memory accesses (A[B[i]] patterns) in scientific computing, graph analytics, and database workloads cause severe DRAM bandwidth underutilization because DRAM controllers have only a 32–128 request window to reorder commands, while the dependency chains of indirect loads limit the memory-level parallelism achievable by conventional cores. Prior prefetchers and fetcher units improve latency but do not reorder, coalesce, or interleave accesses for bandwidth efficiency.
method: DX100 is a programmable, memory-mapped accelerator shared across CPU cores that offloads bulk indirect and streaming memory operations. An 8-instruction ISA supports indirect loads/stores/RMWs, streaming loads/stores, ALU operations, and range-loop fusion. The Indirect Access unit uses a Row Table (BCAM + SRAM) to reorder up to 16K indices per tile for DRAM row-buffer hit maximization, a Word Table for coalescing redundant column accesses, and a Request Generator that interleaves requests across DRAM channels and bank groups. Streaming accesses go to the LLC via Cache Interface; indirect accesses bypass the cache hierarchy and inject directly into DRAM controllers, with a Coherency Agent maintaining cache coherence by snooping directories during the fill stage. An MLIR-based compiler (using Polygeist for C/C++ lowering) automatically detects indirect accesses, performs loop tiling, hoists bulk operations, and emits DX100 API calls—covering over 99% of graph frontier nodes across evaluated benchmarks.

title: SwiftVI: Faster Value Iteration via Heap-Based Action Elimination
problem: Standard value iteration (VI) for large Markov Decision Processes is computationally expensive because it updates all state-action pairs every iteration, even when most actions can be provably pruned.
method: Maintains a max-heap of action upper bounds per state; after each value update, eliminates actions whose upper bounds fall below the current best lower bound. Combines four algorithmic variants: VIH (heap only), VIAE (asynchronous elimination), VIAEH (hybrid), VIAEHL (with lookahead), all exploiting monotone value function structure.

title: LUT Tensor Core: A Software-Hardware Co-Design for LUT-Based Low-Bit LLM Inference
problem: Low-bit LLM inference (INT4/2/1 weights × FP16/INT8 activations) requires mixed-precision GEMM (mpGEMM), an operation not natively supported by existing GPU Tensor Cores, forcing inefficient dequantization-based workarounds. Lookup-table (LUT) approaches can in principle replace multiplications with table lookups, but conventional LUT hardware incurs prohibitive table precomputation and storage overhead that negates the area and efficiency gains.
method: LUT Tensor Core is a software-hardware co-design: on the software side, table precomputation is extracted into an independent kernel via dataflow graph (DFG) transformation and fused with the preceding element-wise operator to eliminate redundant computation; weight values are reinterpreted from {0,1} to {-1,+1} to exploit lookup table symmetry and halve storage. On the hardware side, a bit-serial LUT Tensor Core microarchitecture with an elongated MNK tiling shape (M=2, N=64, K=4 optimal) maximizes table reuse across the N dimension while keeping table size bounded; a dedicated LMMA instruction set extends existing MMA ISA and integrates with TVM/Roller/Welder compilation stacks for end-to-end kernel generation.

title: ScaleFusion: Scalable Inference of Spatial-Temporal Diffusion Transformers for High-Resolution Long Video Generation
problem: Existing sequence parallelism techniques (DeepSpeed-Ulysses, RingAttention, DSP) for distributed ST-DiT inference incur 34-44% communication overhead when crossing machine boundaries, preventing efficient strong scaling beyond a single server.
method: ScaleFusion exploits spatial-temporal independence: spatial attention is independent along the temporal dimension, and temporal attention is independent along the spatial dimension. This allows slicing each layer execution into NT temporal slices (spatial layers) or NS spatial slices (temporal layers). Intra-layer scheduling: execute all-to-all for slice i+1 asynchronously while computing slice i (pipelining communication and computation within a layer). Inter-layer scheduling: further decompose the first slice's all-to-all into LT or LS sub-partitions, and lift 2/3 of them to overlap with the last-slice computation of the previous layer, eliminating the head and tail of the pipeline that can't be overlapped by intra-layer alone. Two CUDA streams (compute and communication) are used. Hyperparameters NT=NS=4, LT=1, LS=3 are used by default.
